claim: The ventral tenia tecta (vTT) is a component of the olfactory cortex.
source: The ventral tenia tecta (vTT) is a component of the olfactory cortex and receives both bottom-up odor signals and top-down signals.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract of the manuscript.

claim: The vTT receives both bottom-up odor signals and top-down signals.
source: The ventral tenia tecta (vTT) is a component of the olfactory cortex and receives both bottom-up odor signals and top-down signals.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract.

claim: Individual vTT cells are highly tuned to a specific behavioral epoch of learned tasks.
source: We report that individual vTT cells are highly tuned to a specific behavioral epoch of learned tasks, whereby the duration of increased firing correlated with the temporal length of the behavioral epoch.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The duration of increased firing in vTT cells correlated with the temporal length of the behavioral epoch.
source: We report that individual vTT cells are highly tuned to a specific behavioral epoch of learned tasks, whereby the duration of increased firing correlated with the temporal length of the behavioral epoch.
evidence: This correlation is demonstrated in Figure 4A showing r = 1.00, p<10−3.

claim: The peak time for increased firing among recorded vTT cells encompassed almost the entire temporal window of the tasks.
source: The peak time for increased firing among recorded vTT cells encompassed almost the entire temporal window of the tasks.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 4B.

claim: vTT cells are selectively activated during a specific behavioral context.
source: Collectively, our results indicate that vTT cells are selectively activated during a specific behavioral context and that the function of the vTT changes dynamically in a context-dependent manner during goal-directed behaviors.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The function of the vTT changes dynamically in a context-dependent manner during goal-directed behaviors.
source: Collectively, our results indicate that vTT cells are selectively activated during a specific behavioral context and that the function of the vTT changes dynamically in a context-dependent manner during goal-directed behaviors.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the observed neural activity patterns across different behavioral contexts.

claim: Odor signals detected by sensory neurons in the olfactory epithelium are transmitted via the olfactory bulb to the olfactory cortex in mammals.
source: In mammals, odor signals detected by sensory neurons in the olfactory epithelium are transmitted via the olfactory bulb to the olfactory cortex.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of olfactory neuroscience.

claim: Mitral and tufted cells in the olfactory bulb send axonal projections to various areas of the olfactory cortex.
source: Mitral and tufted cells in the olfactory bulb send axonal projections to various areas of the olfactory cortex (Igarashi et al., 2012; Neville and Haberly, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The vTT is a relatively unexplored area of the olfactory cortex located in the ventromedial aspect of the olfactory peduncle.
source: In the present study, we examined how the ventral tenia tecta (vTT), a relatively unexplored area of the olfactory cortex located in the ventromedial aspect of the olfactory peduncle, transforms the perception of odor signals into reward-directed behaviors.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the anatomical location and research status of the vTT.

claim: Neocortical sensory area neurons receive sensory signals from the environment as well as top-down signals generated internally by higher order cognitive and behavioral decision processes.
source: Physiological studies of the visual, auditory, and somatosensory cortices have revealed that neocortical sensory area neurons receive sensory signals from the environment, as well as top-down signals that are generated internally by higher order cognitive and behavioral decision processes, including attention, reward-prediction, working memory, and behavioral choice processes (Allen et al., 2019; Gilbert and Sigman, 2007; Roelfsema and de Lange, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research in sensory neuroscience.

claim: Olfactory tubercle neurons encode goal-directed behaviors.
source: In olfactory circuits, olfactory tubercle neurons encode goal-directed behaviors and exhibit enhanced odor responses when animals selectively attend to specific odors (Carlson et al., 2018; Gadziola and Wesson, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Olfactory tubercle neurons exhibit enhanced odor responses when animals selectively attend to specific odors.
source: In olfactory circuits, olfactory tubercle neurons encode goal-directed behaviors and exhibit enhanced odor responses when animals selectively attend to specific odors (Carlson et al., 2018; Gadziola and Wesson, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: c-Fos expression increases in different cells in the olfactory tubercle during distinct motivated behaviors in mice.
source: Furthermore, c-Fos expression (a marker of neuronal activity) increases in different cells in the olfactory tubercle during distinct motivated behaviors in mice (Murata et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The physiological and behavioral functions of the vTT are poorly understood.
source: However, the physiological and behavioral functions of the vTT are poorly understood.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that motivates the current study.

claim: 270 vTT cells were recorded from six mice during the go/no-go task.
source: We recorded the spiking activity of 270 vTT cells from six mice (Tables 1 and 2; recording positions are shown in Figure 1B) while they performed the go/no-go task.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental sample size.

claim: A subset of vTT cells increased their firing rates during the odor presentation phase during both go and no-go trials.
source: We observed that a subset of vTT cells increased their firing rates during the odor presentation phase during both go and no-go trials (an example is shown in Figure 1C).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1C showing example firing patterns.

claim: 68 cells (25% of the recorded cells) significantly increased their firing rates from baseline for five consecutive bins during the odor presentation phase.
source: Using the auROC approach, we defined the odor cue-responsive population (n = 68 cells, 25% of the recorded cells) as cells that significantly increased their firing rates from baseline for five consecutive bins (100 ms) during the odor presentation phase (500 ms after the odor valve opening) in correct go or no-go trials.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the ROC analysis.

claim: No significant differences in the magnitude of firing rate increases between the go and no-go odor cue phases at each time point were observed.
source: No significant differences in the magnitude of these increases between the go and no-go odor cue phases at each time point were observed (bottom lines in Figure 1D, p>0.01, Welch's t test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from comparing firing rates between conditions.

claim: The activity of vTT cells was strongly correlated between go and no-go odor cue presentation phases.
source: This analysis revealed that the activity of vTT cells was strongly correlated between go and no-go odor cue presentation phases, whereas different cell pairs did not exhibit this correlation (bottom lines in Figure 1E, p<10−13, two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Individual vTT cells did not represent odor cue differences between go and no-go trials during odor presentation phases.
source: These results suggest that individual vTT cells did not represent odor cue differences between go and no-go trials during odor presentation phases.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the lack of differential firing between go and no-go trials during odor presentation.

claim: The median duration of nose pokes after the onset of odor stimulation was 839 ms in the go trials.
source: The median duration of nose pokes after the onset of odor stimulation was 839 ms (interquartile range: 703–1003 ms) in the go trials and 738 ms (interquartile range: 621–946 ms) in the no-go trials (57 sessions from six mice).
evidence: This is a quantitative behavioral measurement from the experiments.

claim: The median duration of nose pokes after the onset of odor stimulation was 738 ms in the no-go trials.
source: The median duration of nose pokes after the onset of odor stimulation was 839 ms (interquartile range: 703–1003 ms) in the go trials and 738 ms (interquartile range: 621–946 ms) in the no-go trials (57 sessions from six mice).
evidence: This is a quantitative behavioral measurement from the experiments.

claim: 7% of vTT cells exhibited tuning peak times within the time window of the approach epoch.
source: Of vTT cells, 7% exhibited tuning peak times within the time window of the approach epoch, indicating a significantly greater probability of exhibiting an increase in firing rate during the approach epoch
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cell classification analysis.

claim: 24% of vTT cells had tuning peak times during the odor-sampling epoch.
source: 24% had tuning peak times during the odor-sampling epoch, indicating that the firing rates of these cells were increased during the odor-sampling epoch
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cell classification analysis.

claim: 23% of vTT cells had tuning peak times during the moving epoch.
source: 23% and 11% had tuning peak times during the moving and waiting epochs, respectively, indicating that these cells were tuned to each epoch
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cell classification analysis.

claim: 11% of vTT cells had tuning peak times during the waiting epoch.
source: 23% and 11% had tuning peak times during the moving and waiting epochs, respectively, indicating that these cells were tuned to each epoch
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cell classification analysis.

claim: 15% of vTT cells had tuning peak times during the drinking epoch.
source: and 15% had tuning peak times during the drinking epoch, indicating that they were tuned to the drinking epoch.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cell classification analysis.

claim: Individual vTT cells tended to decrease their activity during other behavioral epochs.
source: Moreover, we observed that these classified cells tended to decrease their activity during other behavioral epochs, suggesting that individual vTT cells exhibit distinct tuning profiles for specific goal-directed behaviors.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and visible in Figure 2B.

claim: 374 vTT cells were recorded from six mice during the odor-guided eating/no-eating task.
source: We recorded spike activity from 374 well-isolated vTT cells from six mice (Tables 3 and 4, recording positions are depicted in Figure 3—figure supplement 1) while mice performed the odor-guided eating/no-eating task.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental sample size.

claim: 19% of vTT cells had tuning peak times during the approach epoch in the eating/no-eating task.
source: These analyses revealed that 19%, 20% and 12% of vTT cells had tuning peak times during the approach, eating and food removal epochs, respectively, suggesting that these three cell classes were tuned to specific and distinct behaviors.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cell classification analysis.

claim: 20% of vTT cells had tuning peak times during the eating epoch in the eating/no-eating task.
source: These analyses revealed that 19%, 20% and 12% of vTT cells had tuning peak times during the approach, eating and food removal epochs, respectively, suggesting that these three cell classes were tuned to specific and distinct behaviors.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cell classification analysis.

claim: 12% of vTT cells had tuning peak times during the food removal epoch in the eating/no-eating task.
source: These analyses revealed that 19%, 20% and 12% of vTT cells had tuning peak times during the approach, eating and food removal epochs, respectively, suggesting that these three cell classes were tuned to specific and distinct behaviors.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cell classification analysis.

claim: A significant difference in firing rate increases was observed between vanilla essence and powder chow presentations during the eating epoch.
source: A significant difference in firing rate increases between vanilla essence and powder chow presentations was observed.
evidence: This is a statistical result shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: No significant difference was observed in firing rate increases between eugenol and vanilla essence presentation during the eating epoch.
source: No significant difference was observed in firing rate increases between eugenol and vanilla essence presentation or between eugenol and powder chow presentation, implying that vTT cells increase their firing during eating epoch behaviors in a manner largely independent of the type of odor cue.
evidence: This is a statistical result from comparing firing rates across odor conditions.

claim: No significant differences in baseline firing rates were observed between tasks.
source: No significant differences in baseline firing rates were observed between tasks (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, p>0.05, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from comparing baseline firing rates.

claim: No significant differences were noted in mean firing rates in the classified cell populations during each of the most preferred epochs.
source: No significant differences were noted in mean firing rates in the classified cell populations during each of the most preferred epochs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, p>0.05, Tukey's test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from comparing mean firing rates across cell groups.

claim: The median for neural tuning durations was positively correlated with that of behavioral epoch durations (r = 1.00, p<10−3).
source: The median for neural data was positively correlated with that of behavioral data (r = 1.00, p<10−3, Figure 4A), suggesting that the duration of sustained discharge in vTT cells was dependent on the duration of the behavioral epoch.
evidence: This is a statistical result showing a strong correlation between neural and behavioral durations.

claim: The duration of sustained discharge in vTT cells was dependent on the duration of the behavioral epoch.
source: The median for neural data was positively correlated with that of behavioral data (r = 1.00, p<10−3, Figure 4A), suggesting that the duration of sustained discharge in vTT cells was dependent on the duration of the behavioral epoch.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the strong correlation between neural tuning durations and behavioral epoch durations.

claim: The repertoire of vTT tuning peak times encompassed almost the entire continuing series of behavioral epochs for odor-guided reward-directed behaviors.
source: We observed that the repertoire of vTT tuning peak times encompassed almost the entire continuing series of behavioral epochs for odor-guided reward-directed behaviors.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 4B.

claim: More cells had differences in firing rate between the go and no-go trials before the animal exited from the odor port compared to that during the odor presentation phase.
source: When the differences in firing rate were aligned to odor port exit times, we observed that more cells had differences in firing rate between the go and no-go trials before the animal exited from the odor port compared to that during the odor presentation phase (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an observation from the ROC analysis aligned to odor port exit times.

claim: Decoding accuracy was maintained at chance levels during odor presentations and subsequently increased close to the level achieved during behavioral accuracy just before odor port exit.
source: Analyses of the decoding time course based on all 270 cells using a sliding time window revealed that decoding accuracy was maintained at chance levels during odor presentations and subsequently increased close to the level achieved during behavioral accuracy just before odor port exit (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a result from the SVM decoding analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Approximately 86% of vTT cells were Slc17a7-positive.
source: Approximately 86% and 8% of vTT cells were Slc17a7-positive and Gad1/2-positive, respectively, suggesting that the principal neurons of the vTT are glutamatergic.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from in situ hybridization experiments shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Approximately 8% of vTT cells were Gad1/2-positive.
source: Approximately 86% and 8% of vTT cells were Slc17a7-positive and Gad1/2-positive, respectively, suggesting that the principal neurons of the vTT are glutamatergic.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from in situ hybridization experiments shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: The principal neurons of the vTT are glutamatergic.
source: Approximately 86% and 8% of vTT cells were Slc17a7-positive and Gad1/2-positive, respectively, suggesting that the principal neurons of the vTT are glutamatergic.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the high percentage of Slc17a7-positive cells.

claim: The vTT has reciprocal connections with the olfactory bulb (OB), anterior piriform cortex (APC), and posterior piriform cortex (PPC).
source: It has previously been reported that the vTT has reciprocal connections with the olfactory bulb (OB), anterior piriform cortex (APC), and posterior piriform cortex (PPC) (Igarashi et al., 2012; Luskin and Price, 1983a; Luskin and Price, 1983b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The deep layers of the vTT receive top-down inputs from the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC).
source: In addition, the deep layers of the vTT receive top-down inputs from the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) (Hoover and Vertes, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A number of retrogradely labeled (CTB-positive) cell bodies were identified in the OB, APC, PPC, and mPFC after CTB injection into the vTT.
source: A number of retrogradely labeled (CTB-positive) cell bodies were identified in the OB, APC, PPC, and mPFC.
evidence: This is an observation from the retrograde tracing experiments shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: CTB-positive cell bodies were rarely observed in the anterior olfactory nucleus (AON) after CTB injection into the vTT.
source: In contrast, CTB-positive cell bodies were rarely observed in the anterior olfactory nucleus (AON), which is located just dorsal to the vTT (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is an observation from the retrograde tracing experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Many retrogradely labeled vTT cells were observed in mice that received CTB injections in the OB, AON, and APC.
source: Many retrogradely labeled vTT cells were observed in mice that received CTB injections in the OB, AON, and APC.
evidence: This is an observation from the retrograde tracing experiments shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: Only a small number of retrogradely labeled vTT cells were observed in mice that received CTB injections in the OT and PPC.
source: In contrast, only a small number of retrogradely labeled vTT cells were observed in mice that received CTB injections in the OT and PPC.
evidence: This is an observation from the retrograde tracing experiments shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: Retrogradely labeled cells were scarce in the vTT following injections of CTB into the mPFC.
source: Furthermore, retrogradely labeled cells were scarce in the vTT following injections of CTB into the mPFC.
evidence: This is an observation from the retrograde tracing experiments shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: In addition to dense reciprocal connections with the OB, the vTT projects to the AON and APC, and receives top-down projections from the APC, PPC, and mPFC.
source: These results suggest that, in addition to dense reciprocal connections with the OB, the vTT projects to the AON and APC, and receives top-down projections from the APC, PPC, and mPFC (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the connectivity data shown in Figure 6.

claim: 25% of vTT cells exhibited increased firing during the learned odor presentation phases in the odor-guided go/no-go task.
source: In the odor-guided go/no-go task, 25% of vTT cells exhibited increased firing during the learned odor presentation phases (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the ROC analysis.

claim: Many vTT cells exhibited peak firing ~100 ms after odor onset.
source: Although many of these vTT cells exhibited peak firing ~100 ms after odor onset, they did not encode learned odor differences during the odor presentation phases (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is an observation from the temporal analysis of firing patterns.

claim: Firing rate differences in a subset of cells emerged just before the odor port exit during which mice performed behavioral choices.
source: Firing rate differences in a subset of cells emerged just before the odor port exit during which mice performed behavioral choices (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Many vTT cells increased their firing rate before the odor presentation.
source: However, many vTT cells increased their firing rate before the odor presentation (Figures 1D, 2B and 4B), and individual vTT cells exhibited a particular tuning pattern characterized by peak tuning and tuning duration.
evidence: This is an observation from the temporal analysis of firing patterns shown in multiple figures.

claim: The firing activity of vTT cells mainly reflected animal behavior and was dependent on task context.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that the firing activity of vTT cells mainly reflected animal behavior and was dependent on task context.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed firing patterns.

claim: vTT cells exhibited a specific firing rate tuning to each behavioral epoch of the go trials during the odor-guided go/no-go task.
source: During the odor-guided go/no-go task used here (Figure 2), vTT cells exhibited a specific firing rate tuning to each behavioral epoch (e.g. moving to the odor port, odor-sampling in the odor port, moving to the water reward port, waiting for the reward, and obtaining the water reward) of the go trials.
evidence: This is a summary of the results shown in Figure 2.

claim: vTT cells tended to suppress their firing activity during epochs other than the most preferred epoch.
source: Furthermore, these cells tended to suppress their firing activity during epochs other than the most preferred epoch.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of firing patterns across epochs.

claim: Many cells exhibited a short duration of activity at transitions between epochs.
source: Further, many cells exhibited a short duration of activity at transitions between epochs, suggestive of a role in linking the two epochs (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 4B.

claim: vTT cells tuned to the odor-sampling epoch exhibited different activity between go and no-go trials just before odor port withdrawal.
source: Moreover, we observed that vTT cells tuned to the odor-sampling epoch exhibited different activity between go and no-go trials just before odor port withdrawal (Figure 5), implying that individual vTT cells were tuned to a specific time window in task-modulated behavioral contexts rather than to a specific behavior.
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 5.

claim: Individual vTT cells were tuned to a specific time window in task-modulated behavioral contexts rather than to a specific behavior.
source: Moreover, we observed that vTT cells tuned to the odor-sampling epoch exhibited different activity between go and no-go trials just before odor port withdrawal (Figure 5), implying that individual vTT cells were tuned to a specific time window in task-modulated behavioral contexts rather than to a specific behavior.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the context-dependent firing patterns observed.

claim: Each vTT cell has a unique behavior- and context-dependent preference, demonstrated by tuning peak time and tuning duration.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that each vTT cell has a unique behavior- and context-dependent preference, demonstrated by tuning peak time and tuning duration.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the results.

claim: The properties of vTT cells may contribute to the representation of a series of specific behavioral context information during odor-guided behaviors in the vTT.
source: These properties of vTT cells may contribute to the representation of a series of specific behavioral context information (i.e. an episode) during odor-guided behaviors in the vTT.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional role of vTT cells.

claim: vTT cells send their axons to other olfactory cortex areas such as the AON and piriform cortex.
source: As vTT cells send their axons to other olfactory cortex areas such as the AON and piriform cortex (Figure 6; Luskin and Price, 1983a; Luskin and Price, 1983b), we speculate that the vTT may provide information to widespread olfactory areas regarding moment-to-moment changes in behaviors within certain behavioral contexts.
evidence: This is supported by the connectivity data in Figure 6 and citations to previous research.

claim: The vTT may provide information to widespread olfactory areas regarding moment-to-moment changes in behaviors within certain behavioral contexts.
source: As vTT cells send their axons to other olfactory cortex areas such as the AON and piriform cortex (Figure 6; Luskin and Price, 1983a; Luskin and Price, 1983b), we speculate that the vTT may provide information to widespread olfactory areas regarding moment-to-moment changes in behaviors within certain behavioral contexts.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the connectivity and functional data.

claim: Context-dependent modulation of neural activity is observed in mitral cells in the OB during the performance of odor-reinforcer association learning.
source: Indeed, context-dependent modulation of neural activity is observed in mitral cells in the OB, an area that receives direct inputs from the vTT during the performance of odor-reinforcer association learning (Kay and Laurent, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Behavioral context-dependent inputs from other higher-brain areas may contribute to the context-dependent activity of vTT cells.
source: We conjecture that behavioral context-dependent inputs from other higher-brain areas may contribute to the context-dependent activity of vTT cells because it is difficult to explain how behavioral context-dependent activity may otherwise be induced by bottom-up olfactory sensory input alone.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the source of context-dependent activity.

claim: The vTT receives direct top-down inputs from the mPFC and indirect inputs from other olfactory cortical areas.
source: The vTT receives direct top-down inputs from the mPFC and indirect inputs from other olfactory cortical areas (Figure 6; Luskin and Price, 1983b).
evidence: This is supported by the connectivity data in Figure 6 and a citation to previous research.

claim: mPFC neurons are implicated in contextual encoding when animals move between different environmental contexts.
source: In particular, mPFC neurons are implicated in contextual encoding when animals move between different environmental contexts (Hyman et al., 2012) and preferentially fire at a specific position in the trajectory of a maze during a working memory task involving odor place-matching (Fujisawa et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Context-specific activity of the mPFC may contribute to the generation of context-dependent activity in the vTT.
source: Along with the evidence presented here, these findings suggest that context-specific activity of the mPFC may contribute to the generation of context-dependent activity in the vTT.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the connectivity and functional properties.

claim: Odor cue-induced reward-predicting responses occur throughout the brain, including sensory, motor, and prefrontal cortices, as well as subcortical regions.
source: In addition, Allen et al. recently reported that odor cue-induced reward-predicting responses were not restricted to the olfactory cortex but occurred throughout the brain, including sensory, motor, and prefrontal cortices, as well as subcortical regions (Allen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Context-dependent cells are located throughout the brain.
source: This suggests that context-dependent cells are located throughout the brain, and their activity may drive specific information processing modes in the brain.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the cited research.

claim: The vTT may play an important role in entraining specific information processing modes in olfactory areas by acting as a hub, amplifier, or rectifier that sends context-dependent signals from the mPFC to broad olfactory areas.
source: In this regard, the vTT may play an important role in entraining specific information processing modes in olfactory areas by acting as a hub, amplifier, or rectifier that sends context-dependent signals from the mPFC to broad olfactory areas.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional role of the vTT.

claim: The tuning durations of cells classified in the eating epoch showed a bimodal distribution.
source: However, the tuning durations of cells classified in the eating epoch showed a bimodal distribution, whereby some cells exhibited tuning durations that lasted for almost the entire eating epoch, and other cells exhibited short duration phasic responses.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: A subset of vTT cells are tuned to smaller scale behaviors or task elements involving moment-to-moment changes in a particular behavioral context.
source: We speculate that a subset of vTT cells are tuned to smaller scale behaviors or task elements involving moment-to-moment changes in a particular behavioral context.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed diversity in tuning durations.

claim: vTT cells which exhibited peak firing at the transition between epochs may encode the initiation of movement.
source: For instance, vTT cells, which exhibited peak firing at the transition between epochs, especially in the eating/no-eating task, may encode the initiation of movement.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the timing of peak firing.

claim: Many vTT cells increased their firing rates prior to the onset of the most preferred behavioral epochs.
source: During odor-guided goal-directed tasks, many vTT cells increased their firing rates prior to the onset of the most preferred behavioral epochs (Figures 2, 3, 4 and 5).
evidence: This is an observation from the temporal analysis of firing patterns shown in multiple figures.

claim: vTT cell activity is modulated both by signals during ongoing behavior as well as predictions about future behavior.
source: These observations corroborate the idea that vTT cell activity is modulated both by signals during ongoing behavior as well as predictions about future behavior.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the temporal patterns of firing.

claim: vTT cell activity during the prediction of future behaviors was not driven directly by olfactory sensory inputs during ongoing behavior.
source: We speculate that vTT cell activity during the prediction of future behaviors was not driven directly by olfactory sensory inputs during ongoing behavior; rather, it was induced, directly or indirectly, by the piriform cortex and top-down inputs from higher cognitive and motivational centers in the prefrontal cortex (including mPFC) and amygdala.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the source of predictive activity.

claim: vTT cells fired with different intensities according to distinct cue types during the eating epoch of the odor-guided eating/no-eating task.
source: vTT cells fired with different intensities according to distinct cue types during the eating epoch of the odor-guided eating/no-eating task (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The response profiles of vTT cells may be underpinned by changes in the palatability of the reward flavors presented.
source: These response profiles may be underpinned by changes in the palatability of the reward flavors presented, since mice were exposed to both olfactory and taste stimuli during eating.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the differential firing patterns.

claim: The firing patterns of vTT cells are influenced by both external contexts as well as internal states.
source: Based on these results, we speculate that the firing patterns of vTT cells are influenced by both external contexts as well as internal states.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed firing patterns.

claim: Mice were placed on a water restriction schedule of 1–2 mL/day for the odor-guided go/no-go task.
source: For the odor-guided go/no-go task, mice (n = 6) were placed on a water restriction schedule of 1–2 mL/day with daily body weight monitoring to ensure that their body weight remained within 80% of their body weight prior to restriction.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Eugenol was used as the go odor cue in the go/no-go task.
source: Eugenol and amyl acetate (Tokyo Chemical Industry Co., Ltd., Tokyo, Japan) were used as the go and no-go odor cues, respectively.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Amyl acetate was used as the no-go odor cue in the go/no-go task.
source: Eugenol and amyl acetate (Tokyo Chemical Industry Co., Ltd., Tokyo, Japan) were used as the go and no-go odor cues, respectively.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Behavior response accuracies for the cued odor trials and powder chow trials throughout all sessions were 0.93 ± 0.01, 0.90 ± 0.01, 0.96 ± 0.01, and 0.99 ± 0.003 for the eugenol, vanilla essence, almond essence, and powder chow trials, respectively.
source: Behavior response accuracies for the cued odor trials and powder chow trials throughout all sessions were 0.93 ± 0.01, 0.90 ± 0.01, 0.96 ± 0.01, and 0.99 ± 0.003 (mean ± SEM, 63 sessions from six mice) for the eugenol, vanilla essence, almond essence, and powder chow trials, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative behavioral result.

claim: The median baseline firing rates were 2.4 Hz in the go/no-go task.
source: The median baseline firing rates (for the odor-guided go/no-go task, pre-odor cue period, 1.2 to 1 s before odor port entry; odor-guided eating/no-eating task, pre-approach period, 3 to 1 s before the onset of approach behavior) were 2.4 Hz (interquartile range: 1.1–7.0 Hz) (green dashed line) in the go/no-go task (n = 270 cells), and 3.2 Hz (interquartile range: 1.2–7.5 Hz) (yellow dashed line) in the eating/no-eating task (n = 374 cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The median baseline firing rates were 3.2 Hz in the eating/no-eating task.
